rules.rule_en: The subject and verb of a sentence should be in agreement with each other. A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
Two or more singular subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.
When two subjects are joined by 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject.
Either, neither, no, each, every and everyone are followed by a singular verb.
When two singular nouns refer to the same person or thing, the verb must be singular.
When two subjects express one idea, the verb is in the singular.
When a plural noun expresses some specific quantity or amount / units of measurement or time, the verb is in singular.
When two or more singular subjects are connected by 'with', 'together with', 'and not', 'besides', 'no less than', the verb is in singular.
The verb agrees with the number of the nouns that follow the verb.
Some nouns that are plural in form but singular in meaning, take a singular verb.
A plural noun which is in the name of a country, province, or a book, is followed by a singular verb.
A collective noun takes a singular verb.
A relative pronoun must agree with its gender, number and person.
The words between the subject and verb do not affect agreement.

Always Plural: verb after people, police, cattle, a number of, a group of; when subject has two nouns joined by 'and'; after few, many, several, both, all, some; after words like scissors, tweezers, trousers, shorts, jeans, glasses.

Always Singular: verb after 'one of', 'a kind of', 'a type of'; units of measurement and mathematical expressions; when subject has two singular nouns joined by 'or'; nouns connected with each of, each one, either of, neither of, someone, something, anybody, anything, no one, nothing, everybody, everything; names of subjects: mathematics, politics, civics, economics, physics etc.
When two singular nouns joined by 'and' are preceded by 'each' or 'every' the pronoun must be singular and the verb is also singular.
Collective nouns like class, cabinet, committee, board, jury, government, team and staff, take a singular verb when considered a unit, and a plural verb if members are considered individually.
Nouns such as advice, alphabet, brick, clothing, furniture, information, luggage, poetry, scenery, thunder etc. are used only in the singular form and the verb that follows them is also singular.
When 'and' connects two or more titles or designations of the same person, the verb is singular. If the posts are held by two different persons, the verb is plural.
Some nouns denoting money, time and distance take a singular verb, as the specific quantity or amount is considered a whole.
Two or more singular subjects connected by or, nor, either...or, neither...nor, take a singular verb.
When two subjects, one singular and the other plural, are connected by neither...nor, either...or, the verb agrees in person with the subject nearer to it.
When two subjects, one singular and the other plural, are connected by 'as well as', 'with', 'along with', 'together with', the verb agrees with the first subject.
A singular subject takes a singular verb, while a plural subject takes a plural verb.
The verb is always plural after people, police, cattle, a number of, and a group of.
The verb is always plural when the subject consists of two nouns joined by 'and'.
The verb is always plural after few, many, several, both, all, and some.
The verb is always plural after the words: scissors, tweezers, trousers, shorts, jeans, and glasses.
One of, a kind of, and a type of are followed by a singular verb.
Units of measurement and mathematical expressions take a singular verb.
When a subject has two singular nouns joined by 'or', use a singular verb.
Nouns connected with each of, each one, either of, neither of, someone, something, anybody, anything, no one, nothing, everybody, everything take a singular verb.
Names of subjects like mathematics, politics, civics, economics, and physics take a singular verb.
A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
When two singular nouns joined by ‘and’ are preceded by ‘each’ or ‘every’, the verb must be singular.
Collective nouns (class, cabinet, committee, board, jury, government, team, staff) take a singular verb when considered as a unit and a plural verb if members are considered individually.
Nouns such as advice, alphabet, brick, clothing, furniture, information, luggage, poetry, scenery, thunder are used only in singular form and take a singular verb.
When two subjects are connected by 'as well as', 'with', 'along with', or 'together with', the verb agrees with the first subject.
When 'and' connects two titles or designations of the same person, the verb is singular. If the posts are held by two different persons, the verb is plural.
Nouns denoting money, time, and distance take a singular verb when the quantity or amount is considered a whole.
Two or more singular subjects connected by 'or', 'nor', 'either...or', or 'neither...nor' take a singular verb.
When subjects of different numbers (one singular, one plural) are connected by 'either...or' or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
When using 'One of the', the following noun must be in the plural form while the verb remains singular to agree with the subject 'One'.
A collective noun phrase such as 'A bunch of' takes a singular verb.
The phrase 'one of the' is followed by a plural noun.
Subject names ending in 's' (like Mathematics) are treated as singular subjects.
Two items acting as a single unit or meal (Bread and butter) take a singular verb.

examples.input: She is a good speaker.
examples.note_en: Singular subject takes singular verb.

examples.input: Children are playing.
examples.note_en: Plural subject takes plural verb.

examples.input: You and I love music
examples.note_en: Two singular subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.

examples.input: Her cousins as well as she are hard working.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with the first subject.

examples.input: Each of them is lovable
examples.note_en: Each takes a singular verb.

examples.input: Peanut butter and jelly is my favourite sandwich.
examples.note_en: Subjects express one idea.

examples.input: Thirty litres of milk is too much for payasam.
examples.note_en: Specific quantity/amount takes singular.

examples.input: He and not she
examples.note_en: Handwritten notes: 'plenty of' count; 'advice' is singular.

examples.input: There ____ ten students in the crowd.
examples.note_en: The verb agrees with the number of the nouns that follow.

examples.input: News ____ never comes too late.
examples.note_en: Handwritten notes: 'physics', 'maths'.

examples.input: Around the World in Eighty Days ____ an adventure novel.
examples.note_en: Title of a book takes a singular verb.

examples.input: The whole class ____ attentive.
examples.note_en: Handwritten note: 'Abstract', 'or plu -> committee'.

examples.input: It is I, who ____ to write.
examples.note_en: Relative pronoun agreement.

examples.input: The little girl, who is wearing gloves, ____ well dressed.
examples.note_en: Words between subject and verb do not affect agreement.

examples.input: The team is performing well. / The staff are arguing about the dates of the tour programme.
examples.note_en: Collective noun 'team' acting as unit takes singular, 'staff' acting as individuals takes plural.

examples.input: The scenery of Kashmir is enchanting.
examples.note_en: Scenery is treated as a singular noun.

examples.input: The Correspondent and Principal has called for a meeting. / The Correspondent and the Principal are attending a meeting.
examples.note_en: Singular verb for same person holding two titles; plural for two different people.

examples.input: Five rupees has no value these days.
examples.note_en: Money amount as a whole takes singular verb.

examples.input: Either Ramesh or Naren is in the wrong.
examples.note_en: Concord rule for Either-Or.

examples.input: Kumar, as well as his friends, has won the prize.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with first subject 'Kumar'.

examples.input: The captain, with all his sailors, was drowned.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with first subject 'captain'.

examples.input: The students along with their teacher, have gone on a visit to the Museum.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with first subject 'students'.

examples.input: Either Shyam or Ram has to pay the fine.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with the closer subject in either/or constructions.

examples.input: Abdul as well as Karim deserves praise.
examples.note_en: When using 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject.

examples.input: Ten thousand rupees a month is an insufficient income.
examples.note_en: A sum of money, even if plural in form, takes a singular verb when considered a single unit.

examples.input: Many a student was awarded at the function.
examples.note_en: The phrase 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb.

examples.input: Neither Veena nor his sisters have been informed of the accident.
examples.note_en: In 'neither/nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

examples.input: My scissors are missing.
examples.note_en: Some nouns like 'scissors' are always treated as plural.

examples.input: Sixty miles is a long distance.
examples.note_en: A distance, though plural in form, is treated as a singular unit.

examples.input: Rekha and her sisters (watch, watches) television everyday.
examples.note_en: Compound subject with 'and' takes plural verb.

examples.input: One of the cookies (is, are) missing.
examples.note_en: Rule: 'One of' takes singular verb.

examples.input: A lady with ten cats (live, lives) in that big house.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with the head noun 'lady'.

examples.input: Measles (is, are) very serious.
examples.note_en: Noun in plural form takes singular verb.

examples.input: Everybody (enjoy, enjoys) a good song.
examples.note_en: Rule: 'Everybody' takes singular verb.

examples.input: Hacking generally refers to unauthorized intrusion...
examples.note_en: Singular subject 'Hacking' takes singular verb 'refers'.

examples.input: The person engaged in hacking activities is known...
examples.note_en: Singular subject 'person' takes singular verb 'is'.

examples.input: This hacker may alter system or security features...
examples.note_en: Modal verb 'may' remains constant; singular subject 'hacker' is compatible with the construction.

examples.input: Hackers employ a variety of techniques.
examples.note_en: Plural subject 'Hackers' takes plural form verb 'employ'.

examples.input: Confidential Data such as Banking username... should not be stored...
examples.note_en: Subject 'Data' takes plural auxiliary 'should'.

examples.input: Every citizen
examples.note_en: Singular subject takes singular verb.

examples.input: All citizens
examples.note_en: Plural subject takes plural verb.

examples.input: Every man and every woman
examples.note_en: Singular nouns with 'every' take singular verb.

examples.input: The team
examples.note_en: Collective noun usage depending on context.

examples.input: His luggage
examples.note_en: Uncountable/Singular nouns like luggage take singular verb.

examples.input: Either Rahim or his brothers have to be invited.
examples.note_en: Verb agrees with the nearer subject (his brothers).

examples.input: One of the body looks sad.
examples.output: One of the boys looks sad.
examples.note_en: The noun following 'one of the' must be plural (boys), and the verb (looks) agrees with the singular subject 'one'.
